title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Options for DNS Configuration
summary: Specifies IPv6 Router Advertisement options for advertising DNS recursive server addresses and a search list, and obsoletes RFC 6106 with a higher default lifetime for fewer expiries.

plainLanguage.summary:
An IPv6 router already sends a message to the hosts on its link to tell them about addresses and prefixes. This RFC adds two more pieces of information to that same message: which DNS servers to ask, and which domain endings to try when a name is given without a full domain.

Both carry an expiry time, so a host knows when to stop using them. The change from the previous version of this document is a longer default expiry, so the information survives on links that lose packets.

questions: ipv6 router advertisement dns option type
subtitle: How an IPv6 router tells hosts which DNS servers and search domains to use, inside the Router Advertisement it already sends.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 host that configures its own address needs to know which DNS servers to use and which domain suffixes to try. DHCPv6 can carry that, but a network with no DHCPv6 infrastructure, or with hosts that have no DHCPv6 client, would leave those hosts without a way to resolve names.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two options for the IPv6 Router Advertisement: one listing the addresses of recursive DNS servers and one listing the DNS search list. Both carry a lifetime, so the host knows how long the information stays valid.
tldr.outcome: A host can configure its address and its DNS settings from the same advertisement, with no DHCPv6 needed. The RFC obsoletes RFC 6106 and raises the default lifetime of the options so they survive on lossy links.

today: RFC 8106 is a Proposed Standard from March 2017. It obsoletes RFC 6106 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The main change from the earlier document is a higher default lifetime for the two options, so that they do not expire on links with a high rate of packet loss.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The purpose of the document is to standardize IPv6 Router Advertisement options for DNS Recursive Server Addresses used for DNS name resolution in IPv6 hosts, and for a DNS Search List of domain suffixes.

IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration provide ways to configure nodes with one or more IPv6 addresses, default routers and other parameters. It is infeasible to configure nomadic hosts manually each time they connect to a different network, and a one-time static configuration is generally not desirable on general-purpose hosts such as laptops. For instance, locally defined namespaces would not be available to the host if it were to run its own recursive name server directly connected to the global DNS.

The DNS information can also be provided through DHCPv6. However, access to DNS is a fundamental requirement for almost all hosts, so IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration cannot stand on its own as an alternative deployment model in any practical network without some support for DNS configuration. These issues are not pressing in dual-stack networks as long as a DNS server is available on the IPv4 side, but they become more critical with the deployment of IPv6-only networks.

RA-based DNS configuration is a useful alternative in networks where an IPv6 host's address is autoconfigured and where either there is no DHCPv6 infrastructure at all or some hosts do not have a DHCPv6 client. For networks that need to distribute additional information, DHCPv6 is likely to be employed, and in those networks RA-based DNS configuration may not be needed. The host learns its DNS configuration from the same Router Advertisement that provides configuration information for the link.

The two mechanisms, the RA options here and the DHCPv6 options, can be used together. Hosts conforming to this specification must extract DNS information from Router Advertisement messages, unless static DNS configuration has been specified by the user. If DNS information is available from multiple Router Advertisements and or from DHCP, the host must maintain an ordered list of that information.
sections.plainLanguage: The point is that a host should not need a DHCP server just to look up names. If the router already tells the host its address, it can tell it where the DNS servers are too.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The document uses the terminology of Neighbor Discovery and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration, and defines six new terms.

A Recursive DNS Server is a server that provides a recursive DNS resolution service for translating domain names into IP addresses or resolving PTR records. The RDNSS Option is an IPv6 Router Advertisement option that delivers the RDNSS information to IPv6 hosts.

The DNS Search List is the list of DNS suffix domain names used by IPv6 hosts when they perform DNS query searches for short, unqualified domain names. The DNSSL Option is an IPv6 Router Advertisement option that delivers that list.

The DNS Repository is a pair of data structures for managing DNS configuration information in the IPv6 protocol stack, in addition to the Neighbor Cache and Destination Cache for Neighbor Discovery. The first data structure is the DNS Server List for RDNSS addresses, and the second is the DNSSL for DNS search domain names.

The Resolver Repository is the configuration repository with RDNSS addresses and a DNSSL that a DNS resolver on the host uses for DNS name resolution, for example the UNIX resolver file and the Windows registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The host keeps two copies of the router's information: one for the protocol stack and one for the resolver that actually looks names up. The RFC is mostly about keeping those two in step.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The document standardizes a Neighbor Discovery option called the RDNSS option, which contains the addresses of recursive DNS servers, and an option called the DNSSL option, which contains the DNS search list. This is to maintain parity with the DHCPv6 options and to ensure that there is necessary functionality to determine the search domains.

The existing Neighbor Discovery message, the Router Advertisement, is used to carry this information. Through the RDNSS and DNSSL options, along with the Prefix Information option, an IPv6 host can perform the network configuration of its IPv6 address and its DNS information simultaneously without needing DHCPv6 for the DNS configuration. The options can be used on networks that support Neighbor Discovery.

This approach requires manual configuration, or automatic mechanisms such as DHCPv6 or vendor-specific mechanisms, to configure the DNS information in the routers sending the advertisements. The automatic configuration of RDNSS addresses and a DNSSL in routers is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Two options, one message, no extra round trip. The router still has to be told what to advertise, but once it knows, every host on the link picks it up from the advertisements it was already receiving.

sections.title: The Recursive DNS Server Option
sections.content:
The RDNSS option contains one or more IPv6 addresses of recursive DNS servers. All of the addresses share the same Lifetime value; if different lifetimes are desirable, multiple RDNSS options can be used.

The Type field is the 8-bit identifier of the option type as assigned by IANA, which is 25. The Length field is an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the length of the option, including the Type and Length fields, in units of 8 octets. The minimum value is 3 if one IPv6 address is contained in the option, and every additional RDNSS address increases the length by 2. The receiver uses the Length field to determine the number of IPv6 addresses in the option, which is equal to (Length - 1) / 2.

The Lifetime field is a 32-bit unsigned integer giving the maximum time in seconds, relative to the time the packet is received, over which these RDNSS addresses may be used for name resolution. The value should by default be at least three times the maximum Router Advertisement interval, as defined in Neighbor Discovery. A value of all one bits represents infinity, and a value of zero means that the RDNSS addresses must no longer be used.

The addresses of the recursive DNS servers are one or more 128-bit IPv6 addresses. They may be link-local addresses; such link-local addresses should be registered in the Resolver Repository along with the corresponding link zone indices of the links that receive the option for them, and a resolver sending a query to a link-local address must use the corresponding link.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small header followed by the server addresses. The header says how many addresses follow and how long they may be used for.

sections.title: The DNS Search List Option
sections.content:
The DNSSL option contains one or more domain names of DNS suffixes. All of the domain names share the same Lifetime value, and multiple DNSSL options can be used if different lifetimes are desirable.

The Type field is 31. The Length field is an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the length of the option in units of 8 octets; the minimum value is 2 if at least one domain name is contained in the option, and the field is set to a multiple of 8 octets to accommodate all the domain names.

The Lifetime field is a 32-bit unsigned integer with the same semantics as in the RDNSS option: the maximum time in seconds, relative to the time the packet is received, over which the domain names may be used for name resolution, a default of at least three times the maximum Router Advertisement interval, all one bits meaning infinity and zero meaning the names must no longer be used.

The domain names must be encoded as a sequence of labels ending in a zero octet, and the representations of several names are concatenated as they are. The domain names must not be encoded in the compressed form. Because the size of the field must be a multiple of 8 octets, the remaining octets other than the encoding parts of the domain name representations are padded with zeros.
sections.plainLanguage: The search list option has the same shape as the server option, but carries domain names instead of addresses. The names are stored one after another, each ending with a zero byte.

sections.title: The DNS Configuration Procedure
sections.content:
The procedure for DNS configuration through the RDNSS and DNSSL options is the same as it is with any other Neighbor Discovery option. When an IPv6 host receives DNS options through Router Advertisement messages, it checks their validity with the Length field: the Length in the RDNSS option must be at least 3 and satisfy (Length - 1) % 2 == 0, and the Length in the DNSSL option must be at least 2. The validity of the RDNSS option is also checked against the addresses field, which should hold unicast addresses.

If the options are valid, the host should copy their values into the DNS Repository and the Resolver Repository in that order. Otherwise the host must discard them.

Where the DNS information can be obtained from multiple sources, such as Router Advertisements and DHCP, the host should keep some options from all sources. Unless explicitly specified for the discovery mechanism, the exact number of addresses and domain names to keep is a matter of local policy, but the ability to store a total of at least three RDNSS addresses or DNSSL domain names from the multiple sources is recommended. The options from RAs and DHCP should be stored so that information from DHCP appears first and therefore takes precedence. For DNS options announced by RAs, those that use the Secure Neighbor Discovery protocol must be preferred over those that do not, and options announced by RAs via Secure Neighbor Discovery must be preferred over those announced by unauthenticated DHCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The host checks that the option is well formed before using it, and keeps what it has learned from more than one source, with DHCP winning over plain router advertisements and signed advertisements winning over unsigned ones.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Two data structures should be synchronized with the Resolver Repository: the DNS Server List, which keeps the list of RDNSS addresses, and the DNSSL, which keeps the list of DNS search domain names. Each entry in these lists consists of a pair of an RDNSS address or DNSSL domain name and an Expiration-time, which is the time when the entry becomes invalid. The Expiration-time is set to the value of the Lifetime field of the option plus the current time, and is updated when a new option with the same address or domain name arrives on the same interface. The DNS information need not be dropped when the expiry of the Router Advertisement router lifetime happens, because these options have their own lifetime values.

Processing an RDNSS option has four steps. The addresses are parsed from the option. If an address already exists in the DNS Server List and the option's Lifetime field is set to zero, the entry is deleted from both the DNS Server List and the Resolver Repository, which is how a resolver resigns from its DNS service or how a renumbering scenario retires an old address. If the address already exists and the Lifetime is not zero, only the Expiration-time is updated. If the address does not exist, it is registered and inserted as the first one in the Resolver Repository, and if the list is full the entry with the shortest Expiration-time is deleted from both places. The ordering of addresses within one option is preserved in the Resolver Repository, so that they are preferred in the order the router gave them.

When an entry expires in the DNS Server List, the expired entry is deleted from it and the corresponding address is deleted from the Resolver Repository. The processing of the DNSSL option is the same as the processing of the RDNSS option.
sections.plainLanguage: The host keeps its own list of what it has been told, with an expiry time for each entry, and mirrors that list into the resolver's configuration. A router that withdraws a server does so by advertising a zero lifetime, and the host then drops it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For the RDNSS option, an attacker could send a Router Advertisement with a fraudulent RDNSS address, misleading IPv6 hosts into contacting an unintended DNS server for name resolution. For the DNSSL option, an attacker can let IPv6 hosts resolve a hostname without a DNS suffix into an unintended host's IP address with a fraudulent search list. These attacks are similar to the Neighbor Discovery attacks that use Redirect or Neighbor Advertisement messages to redirect traffic to addresses of malicious parties.

However, the security of these options for DNS configuration does not affect Neighbor Discovery protocol security, because learning DNS information through the options cannot be worse than learning bad router information through the same messages. The vulnerability of Neighbor Discovery is therefore not worse, and is a subset of the attacks that any node attached to a LAN can carry out.

As a recommendation, the Secure Neighbor Discovery protocol can be used to allow all the Neighbor Discovery options, including these two, to be automatically signed with digital signatures. It is common for network devices such as switches to include mechanisms that block unauthorized ports from running a DHCPv6 server, to provide protection from rogue DHCPv6 servers; the corresponding technique for network devices is recommended to block rogue Router Advertisement messages that include the RDNSS and DNSSL options from unauthorized nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake router on the link could point the hosts at a DNS server of its own. The recommendation is to sign the advertisements, and to have switches drop advertisements carrying these options from ports that are not allowed to send them.

viz.caption: The threats and what answers them

items.title: Fraudulent RDNSS address
items.text: An attacker sends a router advertisement naming a DNS server of their own, so hosts send their lookups there.

items.title: Fraudulent DNSSL
items.text: An attacker sends a search list that resolves a short name into a host of their choosing.

items.title: Secure Neighbor Discovery
items.text: Signing the options lets a host tell a real router from a fake one.

items.title: Router Advertisement guard
items.text: Network devices are recommended to block advertisements carrying these options from unauthorised nodes, the same way they block rogue DHCPv6 servers.
